title: Welcoming questions
hook: welcoming friends of other faiths' questions
tomorrow: Dadi knows things Amira doesn't want to lose. how do you keep them?

segments.voice: Yesterday, no compulsion: share, don't push. But sometimes the pushing comes from the other side of the table.
screen: `SHARE, DON'T PUSH.` → `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: A dining hall, a table of six. Someone asks, kindly enough, why Muslims fast. Before the answer is half done, a guy at the far end cuts in: so you think everyone else is wrong? Now it's a different conversation, and every face at the table turns. Stay, or walk away? The Qur'an has words for both, and Muslims weigh them differently.
screen: `A TABLE OF SIX.` → `A QUESTION, THEN A JAB.` → `STAY, OR WALK AWAY?`

segments.voice: Start underneath both views, with a verse about why people meet at all. In Pickthall's words: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." One human family, spread out on purpose, so that its people would come to know each other. Questions are how knowing starts. Now the two views. View one: stay. The Qur'an says to "reason with them in the better way," and it tells Muslims not to argue with the People of the Scripture except in the best way. Its best case: even a sharp question can be a real one. The guy at the end of the table may be asking about the thing he fears. Walk away, and he keeps his worst guess about you. View two: say peace, and go. The Qur'an praises those "who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace." Its best case: some exchanges aren't questions. They're fights looking for a stage, and feeding them can crowd out the honest asker sitting right there. Both views agree that a real question gets welcomed. They part on how to tell the difference, and that call gets made at the table, not in advance. One for tonight: the verse about nations and tribes gives difference a purpose, and the purpose is knowing one another.
screen: `MADE TO KNOW ONE ANOTHER.` · `STAY: REASON IN THE BETTER WAY.` · `GO: ANSWER, PEACE.` · `A QUESTION, OR A FIGHT?` · then, large: `WELCOME QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Bring back one question someone once asked you about your beliefs, or about something you love, that you answered badly or not at all. Plan the reply you'd give now, in one or two calm sentences. Then run it once in your head, staying kind whether the asker nods or not.
screen: `ONE OLD QUESTION.` · `ONE OR TWO CALM SENTENCES.` · `KIND EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Welcoming questions: treating a real question as a door to knowing one another, and answering peace when it isn't one.
For the road: welcome questions, the honest ones most of all. Day 1753, door open.

howItsDone: Some mosques hold open days and interfaith evenings where neighbors can ask anything, and the answers aim for what the Qur'an calls the better way.

fork.setup: at a family dinner, your cousin's husband, who is Hindu, asks why you pray five times a day. your uncle starts to debate him. you're sitting between them. what do you do?
options: back your uncle up. a question is the chance to win the point.
answer the actual question simply, then ask about his own prayers.
change the subject. faith questions at dinner become fights.
fork.reveal: it was a real question, so view one applies: reason in the better way. and 49:13 says difference is for knowing one another, which goes both ways.

chat.says: Claire's friend asked, half-joking, why i 'let' Islam pick my clothes. answer, or say peace and leave?
options: If it's a real question under the joke, welcome it: answer briefly, then ask hers.
Leave. Saying peace means you never owe anyone an answer to hard questions.
Stay and win it. Reasoning in the better way means proving her wrong.
chat.meaning: The Qur'an says reason in the better way and answer the foolish with peace. A real question gets welcomed; the point is knowing one another (49:13).
